## The big idea

In a static fluid, pressure varies with **elevation only**: $dp/dz =
-\rho g$. Everything else — manometers of any shape, connected reservoirs,
the entire logic of Unit 3 — is that one fact plus bookkeeping. The
bookkeeping rule: *walking down adds $\rho g h$; walking up subtracts it;
walking sideways costs nothing.*

2. How do you read a multi-fluid manometer without memorizing a formula?
3. What makes mercury the classic manometer fluid?

## One derivative rules everything

Isolate a thin horizontal slab of static fluid, thickness $dz$, area $A$.
Vertically, three forces: pressure pushing up on the bottom, $p(z)A$;
pressure pushing down on the top, $p(z{+}dz)A$; and weight, $\rho g A\,
dz$. Static means they balance:

$$\frac{dp}{dz} = -\rho g.$$

(Horizontally, the same argument has no weight term, so no horizontal
variation — which is *why* same depth means same pressure in a connected
fluid, and why the ocean surface is level.) For constant density this
integrates to the workhorse:

$$p_2 = p_1 + \rho g h \qquad (h = \text{depth increase from 1 to 2}).$$

Every hydrostatics result you will ever use is this line wearing
different costumes. In Boulder terms: 10 m of water ≈ 98 kPa ≈ one full
local atmosphere and change — depth is a serious pressure machine.

## Manometry: pressure by walking

A manometer converts a pressure difference into something a ruler can
measure: fluid column heights. To read one, don't hunt for a formula —
**take a walk.** Start at a point of known pressure, traverse the tube to
the point you want, and keep a running tally: descend a height $h$ in a
fluid of density $\rho$, add $\rho g h$; ascend, subtract; move
horizontally within one fluid, change nothing. The tube's *path* —
loops, shelves, spirals — is irrelevant, because only elevation appears
in $dp/dz$. All that matters is the elevation of each fluid *interface*.

Do one, with the tally printed at every station. This cell is yours to
edit — change heights, swap fluids, add a leg:

```{pyodide}
# U-tube: tank of water, mercury manometer leg, open to Boulder air.
# Walk: tank surface -> down through water -> across -> up through mercury -> air
p = 0.0                                  # start: tank surface, 0 gauge
print(f"{'station':38s}{'p (kPa gauge)':>14s}")
print(f"{'A: tank free surface':38s}{p/1000:14.2f}")

p += LIQUIDS['water'] * 9.81 * 1.35      # DOWN 1.35 m of water
print(f"{'B: bottom of water leg (down 1.35 m)':38s}{p/1000:14.2f}")

p -= LIQUIDS['mercury'] * 9.81 * 0.20    # UP 0.20 m of mercury
print(f"{'C: mercury meniscus (up 0.20 m)':38s}{p/1000:14.2f}")

print()
print("...and station C is open to the atmosphere: it SHOULD read 0.")
print("It doesn't -> the tank surface wasn't at 0 gauge. Solve: the tank")
print(f"pressure is {-(p)/1000:.2f} kPa gauge. (The walk works in reverse.)")
```

Notice the trick in the last lines: if the endpoint pressure is known
(open to air = 0 gauge) and the start isn't, run the walk anyway and
solve for the unknown — the tally is just an equation. Notice also why
mercury earns its job: at 13.6× water's density, it compresses large
pressure differences into desk-sized columns. (Measure a 27 kPa
difference in water and you'd need a 2.7 m tube; in mercury, 20 cm.)

::: {.column-margin}
Common assumptions to look out for: "open to atmosphere" → 0 gauge at
that meniscus; gas columns (air above a liquid) → too light to matter,
skip them in the tally; "the fluids don't mix" → each leg keeps its own ρ.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
More tube is not more pressure. A manometer coiled through 10 m of tubing
reads the same as a straight one — column *length* is nothing, interface
*elevation* is everything. If your tally ever includes a horizontal
distance, you've left the physics.
:::

## Earn it — 3 quick gates

Three gates walk a pressure from a pool to a pipe gauge — the daily bread of Unit 3. Ungraded; hints after a miss; **Show me** after two. Arguing about a gate with a classmate is the assignment, not a violation.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-reveal-all"></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Gauge pressure 3.2 m under a pool surface?"
     data-answer="31.3" data-tol="0.03" data-units="kPa"
     data-hint="ρgh, then divide by 1000 for kPa. The ≈9.8 kPa-per-meter exchange rate is worth memorizing."
     data-solution="p = 998 × 9.81 × 3.2 = 31.3 kPa gauge."
     data-target="pm-s2"></div>
```

::: {#pm-s2 .fl-hidden}
Gauge is what the diver's ears feel *extra*. Absolute is what physics (boiling, gas laws) uses:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Absolute pressure at that depth, in Boulder (p_atm = 83 kPa)?"
     data-answer="114.3" data-tol="0.03" data-units="kPa"
     data-hint="Absolute = gauge + local atmosphere — and Boulder's atmosphere is 83, not 101.3."
     data-solution="p_abs = 31.3 + 83.0 = 114.3 kPa. The same dive in Miami reads 18 kPa higher absolute."
     data-target="pm-s3"></div>
```

::: {#pm-s3 .fl-hidden}
Now the workhorse instrument. A mercury U-tube manometer taps a water pipe; the mercury legs differ by 250 mm:

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Pipe gauge pressure indicated?"
     data-answer="30.9" data-tol="0.03" data-units="kPa"
     data-hint="Δp = (ρ_Hg − ρ_water) g h — the water sitting on the near leg buys back some of the mercury's weight. Forgetting the subtraction is the classic."
     data-solution="Δp = (13600 − 998)(9.81)(0.25) = 30.9 kPa."></div>
```

Every manometer in the lab is these three moves in a trench coat.

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** Two open tanks of water sit side by side, connected by a hose at the bottom. One tank is wide, one narrow. Compare pressures at the hose.</summary>
Equal — if the *surface elevations* are equal (and they will be: any
difference drives flow until they match). Width never entered $dp/dz$.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Your manometer walk crosses a 30 cm column of trapped air. How much does it add to the tally?</summary>
About $1.2 \times 9.81 \times 0.3 \approx 3.5$ Pa — versus ~2,900 Pa for
the same height of water. Skipping gas columns isn't laziness; it's a
0.1% decision, and now you know its size.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** An inclined manometer lays its tube at 15° from horizontal. Same fluids, same Δp — what changed, and why do instrument makers bother?</summary>
The fluid must travel $1/\sin 15° \approx 3.9\times$ farther *along the
tube* per unit elevation. The reading is stretched — a sensitivity gain
of ~4× for free. The physics didn't change; the ruler got longer.
</details>
